text.p: It must have been pure golf heaven for avid duffer President Clinton Friday when he attended the opening day of the Presidents Cup tournament, a gathering of some of the biggest names in professional golf.

Clinton spent about five hours at the Robert Trent Jones Golf Club in Lake Manassas, Virginia, site of the 1996 tournament that pits the United States against an international team comprised of players from the rest of the world except Europe.
The president, standing with veteran American golfer Ben Crenshaw under a white awning near the fourth hole, clapped and shook his head in awe at some of the players' shots.
Sipping a soft drink from a can, Clinton, clad in a short sleeve green shirt and tan slacks, at times looked as if he wished he were playing on the lush 7,289-yard, par-72 course.

A veritable who's-who of golf played in the competition, including Corey Pavin, Greg Norman, Fred Couples and Ernie Els. Six of the international members are among the top 20 in world rankings while ten U.S. members are in the top 20.

The international team is captained by five-time British Open champion Peter Thomson, who succeeded fellow Australian David Graham, who was at the helm during the inaugural Presidents Cup matches in 1994.
The American team is headed by Arnold Palmer, who replaced Hale Irwin.
Clinton's presence seemed so far to have helped the United States, which won the tournament 20-12 two years ago.

In various fourball match play, Couples and Davis Love defeated Norman and Robert Allenby 2 and 1; Corey Pavin and Phil Mickelson beat Vijay Singh and Masashi "Jumbo" Ozaki 2 and 1; and David Duval and Mark O'Meara beat Steve Elkington and Frank Nobilo 3 and 2.

The Presidents Cup plays five foursome and five fourball matches on each of the first two days. If it ends in a 16-16 tie Sunday, a playoff will ensue between one player from each team, nominated by the captain.

The honorary chairman of this year's tournament was former President George Bush, who appeared at the event earlier in the day. But the White House said Bush, an avid golfer himself, left before Clinton arrived later in the afternoon.
